content: Neon, represented by the chemical symbol Ne and possessing an atomic number of 10, is a noble gas that is colorless and chemically inert under standard conditions. While it is one of the most abundant elements in the universe, it is relatively rare on Earth. When used in vacuum discharge tubes and neon lamps, neon emits a characteristic reddish glow. Commercially, neon is extracted from the atmosphere, where it exists in trace amounts. Neon was discovered in 1898 by Scottish chemist William Ramsay and English chemist Morris W. Travers in London. The discovery occurred when Ramsay liquefied a sample of atmospheric air, then warmed it to capture the gases released during boiling. Among the gases identified were krypton, xenon, and neon. The isotopes of neon include 20Ne, 21Ne, and 22Ne. Isotopes 21Ne and 22Ne are nucleogenic, and their variations are well understood. However, 20Ne is not nucleogenic, and its variation on Earth has been a subject of significant debate. The primary nuclear reactions responsible for generating neon isotopes involve neutron emission and alpha decay reactions on magnesium isotopes (24Mg and 25Mg), producing 21Ne and 22Ne, respectively. Alpha particles originate from uranium-series decay chains, while neutrons are primarily produced through secondary reactions involving alpha particles. These processes result in lower 20Ne/22Ne ratios and higher 21Ne/22Ne ratios in uranium-rich rocks, such as granites. Isotopic analysis of terrestrial rocks exposed to cosmic rays has demonstrated the cosmogenic production of 21Ne, which is generated through spallation reactions on elements like magnesium, sodium, silicon, and aluminum. By analyzing all three isotopes, researchers can distinguish cosmogenic neon from magmatic and nucleogenic neon, making neon a valuable tool for determining the cosmic exposure ages of surface rocks and meteorites. Neon isotopic content in volcanic gas samples is enriched in 20Ne and nucleogenic 21Ne relative to 22Ne, indicating a non-atmospheric source of neon. The 20Ne-enriched components are attributed to primordial rare gas components, possibly representing solar neon. Elevated 20Ne abundances have also been found in diamonds, further supporting the existence of a solar neon reservoir within the Earth. Neon is the second-lightest noble gas and emits a reddish-orange glow in vacuum discharge tubes. It has over 40 times the refrigerating capacity of liquid helium and three times that of liquid hydrogen on a per-unit-volume basis. In most applications, neon is a more cost-effective refrigerant than helium. Neon plasma produces the most intense light discharge at normal voltages and currents among all rare gases. The light appears red-orange to the human eye but contains a strong green spectral line that is only visible when dispersed by a spectroscope. On a universal scale, neon is the fifth most abundant chemical element by mass, following hydrogen, helium, oxygen, and carbon. Its relative rarity on Earth is due to its lightness and chemical inertness, which prevent it from being trapped in the condensing gas and dust clouds that formed smaller, warmer planets like Earth. Neon’s mass abundance in the universe is approximately 1 part in 750, and in the Sun and the proto-solar system nebula, it is about 1 part in 600. The Galileo spacecraft's atmospheric entry probe found that neon in Jupiter's upper atmosphere is reduced by a factor of 10, to 1 part in 6,000 by mass. This suggests that the ice planetesimals that delivered neon to Jupiter formed in regions too warm to retain neon, even though heavier inert gases are more abundant on Jupiter than in the Sun. Neon is a monatomic gas under standard conditions and is rare on Earth, comprising 1 part in 65,000 by volume or 1 part in 83,000 by mass in the Earth's atmosphere. It is industrially produced through cryogenic fractional distillation of liquefied air. The reddish-orange light emitted by neon in neon lights is widely used for advertising signs and in long tubular strips for car modifications. The term neon is often used generically for these types of lights, even though other gases are used to produce different colors. Neon is also used in vacuum tubes, high-voltage indicators, lightning arrestors, wave meter tubes, television tubes, and helium-neon lasers. Liquefied neon serves as a cryogenic refrigerant in applications that do not require the extremely low temperatures achievable with the more expensive liquid helium. Neon is generally considered chemically inert as a noble gas. However, ions such as Ne+, (NeAr)+, (NeH)+, and (HeNe+) have been observed through optical and mass spectrometric studies. Neon is also known to form an unstable hydrate.
